content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small square or half‑moon pasta parcels filled with a seasoned blend of beef, pork, or a mixture of both. This version is served without sauce, allowing the rich flavor of the meat filling to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli originated in Italy over a thousand years ago and have become a staple of regional cuisines.
Meat‑filled ravioli are often featured in festive meals, especially in northern Italian regions.
The dough is traditionally made from high‑grade flour and eggs, giving it a tender yet firm texture.
When served without sauce, ravioli are commonly drizzled with extra‑virgin olive oil and sprinkled with grated Parmesan.
In some Italian villages the pasta is shaped into tiny stars rather than the classic half‑moon.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in simple carbs
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, the pasta lowers the overall glycemic impact of the dish.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The pasta dough contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If salt is added during preparation, sodium intake should be monitored, especially for those with hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: The meat filling must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C to eliminate harmful bacteria.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Red meat contains saturated fat; moderate consumption is advised for individuals watching cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil the ravioli for 3–4 minutes until al dente, then drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle with grated Parmesan and freshly cracked black pepper. They can also be lightly pan‑fried after boiling for a crisp exterior.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Dry ravioli keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. Cooked ravioli should be cooled, placed in a sealed container, and stored in the refrigerator for no more than 3 days.
